name: The Miami escort's camp, August 1812

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

documented_range.note: Wells arrived on the 12th (Helm), the 13th (Heald) or the 14th (Wau-Bun); the camp opens on Helm's date, the earliest, and closes on the 15th, when the Miamis marched out with the column (Quaife 1913 ch. X). L-1812-gathering-lodges-3499.

change_note: The camp of the Miami escort Wells brought from Fort Wayne, 12-15 August 1812. Added by T-3499; flagged for review.

placement.position_note: NO SOURCE PLACES THE MIAMIS' CAMP; THIS GROUND IS OURS (T-3499). Heald, Helm and Currey say only that Wells came from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miamis 'mounted on ponies' (Currey 1912) and that they marched out on the 15th, part before the column and part behind it (Heald's report, Quaife 1913 Appendix IV). Mounted men come to march the garrison out would camp by the fort, by its stables and the road south they would take, and apart from the Potawatomi gathering on the creek; so the ground stands on the level prairie about 40 m south of the fort's three stables and 175 m south-west of the outer pickets (the owner, 2026-11-08: build the camps 'where they would most logically have been'): local E +1060..+1090, N +56..+80. Its outline lies between -0.01 and +0.04 m of the origin's 2.49 m on the e1830_natural heightfield; it keeps 15 m from every 1812 footprint, 6 m from every worn trail and 4 m from the wagon roads of T-3497 (the fort's south loop and the shore road). The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner. L-1812-gathering-lodges-3499.
placement.symbolic_location: On the prairie about 175 m south-west of the fort: local E +1060..+1090, N +56..+80.

function.note: Helm's narrative (Quaife 1913, Appendix VI): 'Capt. William Wells arrived from Fort Wayne on the 12th August with 27 Miamis and after a council being held by him with the tribes there assembled to amount of 500 warriors 179 women & children'. Wells came from Fort Wayne to bring the garrison out, and his Miamis marched with the column on the 15th, part in the lead and the rest behind (Quaife 1913 ch. X). Where they camped for the two or three nights before is in no source read; that they stood somewhere near the fort is inferred.

citations.citation: J. Seymour Currey, The Story of Old Fort Dearborn. Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912 (published August 1912). A popular history of the first fort from 1803 to its burning in 1812, compiled from the printed accounts and the pioneer recollections before it, with eleven illustrations.
what_it_supplies: two placings of Lee's Place: 'some four miles southwest of the fort ... on the west bank of the South Branch ... about where at the present time the old Illinois and Michigan Canal opens into that stream' (lines 1450-1454), and, in the caption to its illustration, 'on the west bank of the South Branch of the Chicago river some four miles from the mouth of the river' (lines 1484-1486)
the caption of an illustration titled 'Hardscrabble', facing p. 74, which T-2503 is to read as a picture
a 'Map of Chicago in 1812' facing p. 165, not yet opened
the Lee family's house near the fort, on the river bank opposite the mouth, near the later Madison Street and Michigan Avenue, with the sand-bar as the reason (lines 1456-1463)
the Burns house, John Burns's cabin on the north bank near the later State Street bridge, west of the Kinzies' (lines 1565-1576, 2249-2251, 2820-2822)
the four houses left standing on 18 August 1812: the Kinzie and Ouilmette houses, Burns's and Lee's (lines 3100-3105)

the one statement in the corpus that names Guarie among the residents John Kinzie found in 1804 (lines 801-803), uncited; weighed and not followed in data/exclusions.json guarie_trading_house, because Hubbard's tradition, which is Andreas's and Quaife's only authority for Guarie, dates his house before 1778 (T-2489)
what_it_does_not_supply: an eyewitness: Currey writes a century after the farm, from the books before him, and he says so ('it is said in a recent history of Chicago')
a survey distance. 'Some four miles' is a round figure, and the book gives no route for it
the illustration's own date or maker, which the caption does not state; until it is read it is a retrospective picture and grades tier 5 as a picture, whatever this record's tier as a text

research_note: THIS RECORD IS FLAGGED review_required, AND touches_removal, because it draws the camp of Native men at Chicago on the eve of 15 August 1812 from accounts written by the garrison's side; the Miamis, like the Potawatomi, were later removed from their lands. The owner's rulings of 2026-10-16 (AGENTS.md § Standing constraint) trust this project to draw Native depictions on fair and reasonable judgement; the flags stay, and say why here. WHAT IS DRAWN: a small travelling camp in the lodge_camp archetype: two mat lodges and a long lodge of carried mats, two hearths, firewood, a scaffold for saddles and loads, and ten tether stakes for the horses (the Miamis were mounted: Currey 1912, of the battle, 'the mounted Miamis'). The Miamis' own lodge forms are not described at Chicago; the Potawatomi camp's are used as the nearest. NOTHING IS STAGED. WHAT WOULD REPLACE THIS: a source that places or describes the escort's camp. L-1812-gathering-lodges-3499.
